Elizabeth Prentiss
PREN-tiss
proper noun
From the surname Prentiss; a nineteenth-century American author and hymn-writer, author of More Love to Thee, O Christ.

📖 Biblical Definition

Elizabeth Prentiss was a nineteenth-century American author and hymn-writer, the wife of a Presbyterian minister, who knew much of affliction, including the loss of children, and out of her sorrows learned to love Christ the more. She is remembered for the hymn More Love to Thee, O Christ, written in a time of grief, the prayer of a heart that asks for nothing of this world but a deeper love to its Saviour. The dictionary honours Prentiss for setting to song the chief commandment and the chief desire of the sanctified soul, to love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength (Mar 12:30). Her hymn is the cry of one who, in the trial of her faith, more precious than gold that perisheth though it be tried with fire (1Pe 1:7), counted all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus her Lord (Php 3:8). She had learned that nothing can separate the believer from the love of Christ, neither tribulation, nor distress, nor sword (Rom 8:35), and that affliction, sanctified, does not quench but deepens the soul’s love to its Saviour. Her hymn teaches the church to ask, in joy or grief, for more love to Christ above every earthly good.

ELIZABETH PRENTISS, a nineteenth-century American author and hymn-writer.

She was the wife of a Presbyterian minister.

She knew much affliction, including the loss of children.

Her hymn More Love to Thee, O Christ was written in grief.

It is the prayer of a heart that asks only a deeper love to Christ.

📖 Key Scripture

Mar 12:30 — "And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength: this is the first commandment."

1Pe 1:7 — "That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ:"

Php 3:8 — "Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,"

Rom 8:35 — "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Her hymn teaches the church to ask, in joy or grief, for more love to Christ above every earthly good.

expand to see more

What is honourable in Elizabeth Prentiss is the sanctified use she made of affliction. Out of grief and loss she learned to love Christ the more, and gave the church a hymn that asks for nothing of this world but a deeper love to its Saviour. The dictionary honours this hymn of love to Christ, born in the furnace of trial.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that sanctified affliction deepens the soul’s love to Christ rather than quenching it. The first commandment is to love the Lord with all the heart; and the believer, in the trial of his faith more precious than gold, counts all things but loss for the knowledge of Christ. Prentiss had learned that nothing can separate the believer from the love of Christ, and that suffering, received from God’s hand, draws the heart nearer to its Saviour. Her hymn teaches the church to pray, in joy or grief, for more love to Christ above every earthly good.
